body:
## Objective
Implement the two missing mandatory maintenance jobs: `revisit_oldest_modified_candidates` and `revisit_declined_high_potential_candidates`, as defined in Trinity §23.

## Unified Context
The current maintenance cycle applies freshness decay and runs the Icebox promotion. The spec defines two additional mandatory jobs that prevent policy blind spots and rework backlog rot. The oldest-modified candidates are high-value signals: they indicate where the system has stopped progressing, potentially due to policy mismatch or incomplete rework. Declined high-potential candidates represent invested AI compute that should be recovered, not discarded.

## Problem
Without these maintenance jobs:
- Candidates that entered REWORK but were never re-processed accumulate silently
- Items declined months ago with informative feedback never get a second chance
- Policy mismatches that cause systematic blind spots are never detected
- The rework backlog grows without bound, creating invisible technical debt

## Goal
Implement systematic inspection of the two highest-risk candidate populations: oldest-modified items and declined-but-recoverable items.

## In Scope
- `revisit_oldest_modified_candidates(company, context, memory)`: load candidates ordered by `updatedAt ASC`, queue items with unresolved user corrections for REWORK route `OLD_MODIFIED_UNRESOLVED`
- `revisit_declined_high_potential_candidates(company, context, memory)`: load declined candidates, skip hopeless ones, queue recoverable ones for REWORK route `DECLINE_INFORMED_REWORK`
- Hopelessness heuristic: candidate declined more than N times with no intervening memory change
- Integration into the existing `run_maintenance` cycle
- Maintenance run logging: emit counts of queued-for-rework items per job

## Out of Scope
- Full rework execution (queuing is sufficient — the Refiner/Generator handles rework on next cycle)
- UI for maintenance status

## Constraints
- Delivered and Archived items MUST be excluded from revisit candidates
- Maintenance jobs must not starve the main synthesis cycle — apply rate limiting
- Both jobs must emit observable telemetry (log lines or heartbeat fields)

## Acceptance Checks
- [ ] `revisit_oldest_modified_candidates` runs on each maintenance cycle
- [ ] Candidates with unresolved corrections are queued for REWORK
- [ ] `revisit_declined_high_potential_candidates` runs on each maintenance cycle
- [ ] Recoverable declined candidates are queued with route `DECLINE_INFORMED_REWORK`
- [ ] Hopeless candidates (repeat-declined, no memory change) are skipped
- [ ] Both jobs emit counts in maintenance logs

## Dependencies
- #126 Trinity Memory: structured feedback memory

## Delivery Artifact
Two maintenance job implementations integrated into the existing maintenance cycle.
title: Trinity Maintenance: revisit oldest-modified and declined high-potential candidates

body:
## Objective
Refactor the memory layer into a structured, scoped feedback memory system consumable by the Generator, Refiner, Evaluator, and Frontier selector, as defined in Trinity §22.

## Unified Context
The current system injects a flat memory prompt string into AI calls. This prompt is not structured, not scoped by topic or item family, and is not updated from feedback events in a way that changes future behavior. The spec requires memory to produce hard constraints, soft preferences, anti-patterns, duplicate suppression hints, and preferred action patterns — all scoped to GLOBAL, TOPIC, or ITEM_FAMILY levels.

## Problem
Without structured memory:
- Declined items for the same reason reappear because the lesson is not persisted
- Accepted patterns are not reinforced in future generation
- Delivery signals are not fed back to improve which evidence clusters the Generator prioritizes
- All three stages operate on the same flat prompt, regardless of whether lessons are relevant to a specific topic or item family

## Goal
Implement a memory layer that absorbs all feedback event types, distills them into scoped lessons, and makes those lessons consumable by each pipeline stage in a structured way.

## In Scope
- `MemoryEntry` schema: `scope` (GLOBAL/TOPIC/ITEM_FAMILY), `lessonType`, `lessonContent`, `weight`, `createdFrom` (feedback event ID)
- Lesson distillation per event type: DECLINE→negative lesson, MODIFY_ACCEPT→corrective lesson, DELIVER→operational success lesson, ACCEPT→positive pattern lesson
- `process_memory_updates(company)` function consuming unprocessed feedback events
- Stage-specific memory retrieval: each stage pulls relevant lessons by scope
- Hard constraints: patterns that MUST NOT appear again
- Soft preferences: patterns the system SHOULD prefer

## Out of Scope
- Cross-tenant memory
- Vector embedding of memory entries

## Constraints
- Memory MUST be consumable by Generator, Refiner, Evaluator, and Frontier selector
- Feedback that cannot be distilled into a lesson has low system value and should be logged but not stored
- Memory updates must happen asynchronously — not blocking the main synthesis cycle

## Acceptance Checks
- [ ] MemoryEntry schema implemented with scope and lesson type
- [ ] All nine feedback event types produce structured lessons
- [ ] Generator retrieves and applies relevant GLOBAL and TOPIC memory
- [ ] Refiner retrieves duplicate suppression hints from memory
- [ ] Evaluator retrieves anti-patterns and preferred patterns from memory
- [ ] Same decline reason does not reappear after memory updates

## Dependencies
- #125 Trinity Feedback: DELIVER signal and downstream reward propagation

## Delivery Artifact
MemoryEntry schema, lesson distillation per event type, memory retrieval for each pipeline stage.
title: Trinity Memory: structured feedback memory with scoped lessons consumable by all stages

body:
## Objective
Implement the `DELIVER` feedback action as a distinct, stronger signal than `ACCEPT`, and propagate its reward to the full transformation chain that produced the action item, as defined in Trinity §21.

## Unified Context
The current system conflates 'accepting an idea' with 'executing it in reality.' The spec is explicit: DELIVER means the action crossed from suggestion into real execution. This is the strongest positive signal in the system and must have distinct downstream consequences — rewarding not just the action item, but the knowledge lineage, the Refiner path, and the Generator evidence that produced it.

## Problem
Without a DELIVER signal:
- The system cannot distinguish between 'liked but never acted on' and 'actually shipped'
- Transformation paths that produce executed actions receive no stronger reward than ones that produce accepted-but-ignored ideas
- Future generation cannot be weighted toward patterns that have real-world execution track records
- Delivery comments (the richest operational feedback) are not harvested as memory

## Goal
Add DELIVER as a first-class feedback action with distinct state, stronger memory reward, and full lineage propagation.

## In Scope
- `DELIVER` feedback action in the UI (distinct from ACCEPT)
- State transition: item moves to `DELIVERED` state on delivery
- Lineage reward: propagate positive signal to `sourceKnowledgeItemIds`, `generatedFromIds`, and Refiner operation that produced the item
- Delivery comment as high-value memory input
- `lastDeliveredAt` timestamp on action items
- Dashboard: delivered items shown in a separate completed view

## Out of Scope
- Full memory learning layer (separate issue)
- Delivery-to-analytics reporting

## Constraints
- DELIVER must be strictly stronger than ACCEPT in all scoring and memory contexts
- Delivered items must be excluded from the EligibleCandidatePool (they are done)
- Comments on DELIVER must be flagged as high-value memory inputs

## Acceptance Checks
- [ ] DELIVER is available as a distinct UI action on action items
- [ ] Item moves to DELIVERED state and exits the frontier
- [ ] Positive signal is propagated to the source knowledge lineage
- [ ] Delivery comment is persisted and flagged for memory processing
- [ ] Delivered items are excluded from future frontier selection

## Dependencies
- #124 Trinity Feedback: typed decline classification and rework routing

## Delivery Artifact
DELIVER feedback action, DELIVERED state, lineage reward propagation, and delivery comment memory integration.
title: Trinity Feedback: DELIVER signal and downstream reward propagation

body:
## Objective
Implement the `recompute_frontier` function per Trinity §15, replacing the current Icebox 10-item promotion hack with a proper scored frontier selector.

## Unified Context
The current system uses a blunt Icebox promotion: when active tasks drop below 10, the top ICE-scored archived items are promoted. This is not a frontier. The spec defines the Frontier as a strictly-bounded surface of at most 3 items, selected by a multi-factor scoring function from the EligibleCandidatePool, with a three-tier fallback (EVALUATED → REFINED → GENERATED) to ensure the frontier is never empty when any valid candidates exist.

## Problem
Without a proper frontier selector:
- Up to 10 items are surfaced simultaneously, overwhelming the user (spec: max 3)
- Selection is based on ICE score alone — no urgency, freshness, feedback, or strategic priority weighting
- There is no duplicate cluster collapse — two siblings can occupy the frontier simultaneously
- Fallback eligibility is manual (Icebox promotion) instead of automatic and tiered
- The frontier is recomputed only on maintenance cycles, not after every feedback event

## Goal
Implement a formal, scored, de-duplicated, always-non-empty frontier of exactly `min(3, eligible count)` items.

## In Scope
- `recompute_frontier(company, cycleRunId)` function
- Multi-factor frontier score: `stateWeight × qualityWeight × urgencyWeight × freshnessWeight × feedbackWeight × priorityWeight`
- State weights: EVALUATED=1.00, REFINED=0.72, GENERATED=0.45
- Duplicate cluster collapse before ranking
- Rot filter: exclude items past their `rottenAt` threshold
- Three-tier fallback: EVALUATED first, then REFINED, then GENERATED
- Trigger recompute after every feedback event
- Replace Icebox 10-item promotion with this frontier mechanism

## Out of Scope
- Rework routing (separate issue)
- Memory learning

## Constraints
- Frontier MUST NOT exceed 3 items under normal mode (§4)
- Frontier MUST be non-empty when any eligible candidates exist (§24)
- Duplicate siblings MUST NOT occupy the frontier simultaneously

## Acceptance Checks
- [ ] No more than 3 items are surfaced at any time
- [ ] Frontier scoring uses all six weight factors
- [ ] Duplicate cluster siblings do not appear together on the frontier
- [ ] Fallback to REFINED or GENERATED items when EVALUATED pool is insufficient
- [ ] Frontier recomputes after each feedback event
- [ ] Frontier is never empty when eligible candidates exist

## Dependencies
- #122 Trinity Evaluator: relative comparison pool scoring

## Delivery Artifact
`recompute_frontier` function, frontier score computation, cluster collapse, rot filter, and trigger integration.
title: Trinity Frontier: top-3 selector with multi-factor scoring and three-tier fallback

body:
## Objective
Implement the Evaluator as a precision-maximizing stage with relative comparison pool scoring and the six canonical dispositions, as defined in Trinity §10.

## Unified Context
The current Judge stage scores candidates in isolation using only ICE (Impact × Confidence × Ease). The spec requires relative scoring: a candidate can be objectively good but still ineligible because stronger candidates already occupy its decision space. The spec also requires a starvation-safe fallback: an Evaluator that is too strict creates frontier emptiness — a system failure equal to passing junk.

## Problem
Without relative scoring and starvation safety:
- ICE scores are computed in isolation, causing the same decision area to be represented by multiple surfaced items
- Over-strict evaluation creates an empty frontier even when valid candidates exist — the root cause of the original 'No checklist items' bug
- There is no `qualityScore`, `urgencyScore`, or `freshnessScore` — only a single blended ICE number
- Rework cannot be triggered by the Evaluator because it has no `reworkRoute` output

## Goal
Make the Evaluator score each candidate relative to its peer pool and emit a full disposition with all required scoring dimensions. Implement mandatory starvation-safe fallback so the frontier is never empty when eligible candidates exist.

## In Scope
- Relative comparison pool construction per candidate
- Six dispositions: `ELIGIBLE`, `REVISE`, `REGENERATE`, `MERGE`, `SUPPRESS`, `ARCHIVE`
- Full score set per candidate: `qualityScore`, `urgencyScore`, `freshnessScore`, `feedbackScore`, `iceScore`
- Starvation-safe fallback: when supply is starving and `qualityScore >= FALLBACK_THRESHOLD`, force `ELIGIBLE`
- `evaluationReason` field on every evaluated candidate
- `reworkRoute` field set when disposition is `REVISE`, `REGENERATE`, or `MERGE`

## Out of Scope
- Frontier selection (separate issue)
- Memory learning from evaluation results

## Constraints
- An Evaluator that creates frontier starvation is a system failure (§10.7)
- An Evaluator that approves polished low-value artifacts is equally a failure
- Relative dominance must be considered — not only absolute quality

## Acceptance Checks
- [ ] High-quality candidates become `EVALUATED` state
- [ ] Low-support but promising candidates enter `REWORK` with route `REVISE`
- [ ] Fatal duplicates become `SUPPRESSED`
- [ ] Low-quality candidates become `ARCHIVED`
- [ ] When supply is starving, fallback threshold allows marginal candidates through
- [ ] All six scoring dimensions are persisted per candidate
- [ ] Evaluator never creates an empty frontier when eligible candidates exist

## Dependencies
- #118 Trinity: Canonical lifecycle state machine
- #121 Trinity Refiner: full entropy reduction

## Risks
- The starvation-safe fallback is the single most important correctness requirement. Without it, any strict evaluation policy will empty the frontier.

## Delivery Artifact
Updated Evaluator with relative scoring, six-disposition output, and starvation-safe fallback.
title: Trinity Evaluator: relative comparison pool scoring and starvation-safe disposition

body:
## Objective
Implement the Refiner as a genuine entropy-reducing stage with the full operation set required by Trinity §9, replacing the current text-paraphrase-only Writer.

## Unified Context
The current Writer stage only rewrites (paraphrases) candidate text. The spec defines the Refiner as a structural compression stage that must also merge duplicates into stronger candidates, split overloaded candidates into evaluable ones, suppress clearly dominated siblings, and enrich underspecified but promising candidates. A Refiner that only paraphrases text is explicitly called a system failure in §9.9.

## Problem
Without real entropy reduction:
- Semantic duplicates survive into the Evaluator, polluting the ranking pool
- Overloaded candidates (multiple decisions bundled into one) cannot be evaluated fairly
- Weak but promising candidates are discarded rather than enriched
- The Evaluator receives noisy, uncollapsed input and its precision is structurally limited

## Goal
Make the Refiner a real compression stage. For every candidate neighborhood, choose the correct operation and apply it. The output must be a strictly smaller, cleaner, more evaluable set than the input.

## In Scope
- Neighborhood detection: group candidates by semantic similarity (title + body embedding comparison or LLM-based clustering)
- Operation selection: `SUPPRESS_WEAK`, `MERGE`, `SPLIT`, `ENRICH`, `REFINE_AS_IS`
- MERGE: combine semantically overlapping candidates into one stronger candidate, preserving all source lineage
- SPLIT: decompose overloaded candidates into two or more distinct, evaluable candidates
- SUPPRESS: mark clearly dominated siblings as `SUPPRESSED` before evaluation
- ENRICH: strengthen underspecified but promising candidates with contextual grounding

## Out of Scope
- Evaluator scoring
- Frontier selection

## Constraints
- Refiner MUST NOT leave obvious duplicates unresolved (§11.1 mandatory rule)
- Merge must preserve lineage from all merged siblings
- Suppression before evaluation is mandatory to prevent downstream ranking pollution

## Acceptance Checks
- [ ] Exact duplicates are collapsed by SUPPRESS_WEAK
- [ ] Near-duplicates are merged or suppressed based on merge value
- [ ] Overloaded candidates are split into smaller evaluable units
- [ ] Weak but promising candidates are enriched, not discarded
- [ ] All operations preserve candidate lineage
- [ ] Refiner output is strictly smaller in entropy than its input

## Dependencies
- #118 Trinity: Canonical lifecycle state machine
- #119 Trinity: Candidate lineage tracking
- #120 Trinity Generator: multi-cardinality synthesis

## Risks
- Over-compression destroys meaningful distinctions. Under-compression passes through duplicate noise. Both are Refiner failures per §9.9.

## Delivery Artifact
Updated Refiner with neighborhood detection, operation selection logic, and five operation implementations.
title: Trinity Refiner: full entropy reduction (merge, split, suppress, enrich)

body:
## Objective
Add full candidate lineage tracking to all KnowledgeItem and ActionItem records as required by the Trinity spec §8.5 and §9.4.

## Unified Context
Currently the system has no way to trace a surfaced item back through its transformation path. When two items are merged, the loser is discarded without record. When an item is suppressed as a duplicate, there is no cluster ID linking it to its champion. This makes debugging, auditing, and rework-informed improvements impossible.

## Problem
Without lineage:
- Merges destroy provenance — the merged content has no record of where it came from
- Duplicate clusters cannot be managed — the Refiner cannot select a champion if clusters are not tracked
- Rework cannot route correctly — the system cannot find the family of a declined item to enrich or regenerate
- Delivery signals cannot reward the full transformation chain that produced the action

## Goal
Every candidate must carry a complete lineage so the system can trace it back to its evidence source, forward to its derivatives, and laterally to its duplicate siblings.

## In Scope
- `versionFamilyId`: groups all versions of the same conceptual candidate
- `duplicateClusterId`: links semantic siblings detected by the Refiner
- `generatedFromIds[]`: evidence unit IDs that produced this candidate
- `refinedFromId`: the generated candidate this was refined from
- Write lineage on every pipeline stage transition
- Preserve lineage from all members when candidates are merged

## Out of Scope
- Lineage visualization UI
- Cross-tenant lineage

## Constraints
- Lineage must be written atomically with the candidate state transition
- Merge operations must copy `generatedFromIds[]" from all merged siblings to the champion

## Acceptance Checks
- [ ] All four lineage fields exist on KnowledgeItem and ActionItem schemas
- [ ] Generator writes `generatedFromIds[]` on every created candidate
- [ ] Refiner writes `refinedFromId` on every refined candidate
- [ ] Merge operations preserve source lineage from all merged siblings
- [ ] Duplicate cluster IDs are consistent across all siblings in a cluster

## Dependencies
- #118 Trinity: Canonical lifecycle state machine

## Delivery Artifact
Updated schemas, lineage write logic in Generator, Refiner, and merge operations.
title: Trinity: Candidate lineage tracking (versionFamilyId, duplicateClusterId, refinedFromId)

body:
## Objective
Replace the current `DRAFT/CHECKED/VERIFIED/ARCHIVED` status system with the formal Trinity lifecycle state machine as defined in §3.4 of the production definition.

## Unified Context
The current system uses informal statuses (`DRAFT`, `CHECKED`, `VERIFIED`) that do not map to the formal processing stages. This causes the maintenance worker to use heuristic annotation-string matching to infer state — the direct cause of the recent regex catastrophe that was archiving all items system-wide.

## Problem
Without a formal lifecycle:
- Maintenance workers must parse `userAnnotation` strings to determine candidate disposition
- There is no machine-readable signal for whether an item has been through the Refiner or Evaluator
- Fallback and rework routing cannot be implemented reliably
- Stage transitions are not auditable — there is no record of when an item entered each stage

## Goal
Make the candidate lifecycle explicit, finite, and machine-readable. Every item must carry its current state as a typed enum, not inferred from annotation strings.

## In Scope
- New `candidateState` enum: `GENERATED`, `REFINED`, `EVALUATED`, `REWORK`, `SUPPRESSED`, `DELIVERED`, `ARCHIVED`
- `reworkRoute` field: `REVISE`, `REGENERATE`, `MERGE`, `ENRICH`, `DOWNRANK_ONLY`
- Database migration: map existing statuses to new states
- Update all pipeline writes to use the new enum
- Remove annotation-string state inference from maintenance worker

## Out of Scope
- Full rework routing logic (covered in a later issue)
- UI display changes

## Constraints
- Migration must be non-destructive and reversible
- The Icebox auto-promotion logic must be updated to use the new state machine
- No pipeline stage may set state by parsing `userAnnotation` strings after this change

## Acceptance Checks
- [ ] `candidateState` enum is defined in the Prisma schema
- [ ] All existing items are migrated without data loss
- [ ] Generator writes `GENERATED`, Refiner writes `REFINED`, Evaluator writes `EVALUATED`
- [ ] Maintenance worker no longer infers state from annotation strings
- [ ] `reworkRoute` field exists and is set on items entering `REWORK` state

## Dependencies
- #117 Trinity: Canonical Evidence Model

## Risks
- Annotation-string state inference is the current system's single largest reliability risk. This must be eliminated.

## Delivery Artifact
Updated schema, migration script, and updated pipeline stage writes.
title: Trinity: Canonical lifecycle state machine (GENERATED → REFINED → EVALUATED)

body:
## Objective

Add direct user correction controls for flashcards and sources.

## Unified Context

NBA accept/decline feedback is useful, but it is too indirect to fully manage bad knowledge. Users need a direct way to tell the system that a flashcard is wrong, should be hidden, should stay pinned, or that a source should no longer influence generation.

## Problem

Without direct correction controls:
- users can see bad flashcards but cannot correct them directly,
- invalid or low-quality sources can keep re-entering the pipeline,
- the knowledge layer depends too heavily on downstream NBA feedback,
- trust deteriorates when users cannot act on obviously wrong system state.

## Goal

Let users directly correct flashcards and source influence in a way that the local AI pipeline can consume deterministically.

## Scope

### In Scope
- user actions such as:
  - hide flashcard
  - mark flashcard wrong
  - pin flashcard
  - request flashcard refresh
  - ban or suppress a source from future influence
- persistence model for user correction events
- integration of those events into local flashcard refresh logic
- auditability so support can explain why a flashcard is hidden, pinned, or suppressed

### Out of Scope
- full manual flashcard editing workflow
- collaborative moderation or approval queues
- role/permission redesign beyond what is minimally needed for safe corrections

## Execution Prompt

Keep the controls constrained and explainable. The point is not to make users hand-edit the knowledge graph. The point is to give them precise levers when the system is wrong or needs stronger guidance.

## Constraints

- Correction events must be durable and auditable.
- Local processing must consume corrections deterministically.
- A banned source must not silently keep influencing the same company knowledge graph.
- Pinned or hidden state must be explainable in the UI and support tooling.

## Acceptance Checks

- [ ] Users can hide, mark wrong, pin, or request refresh on a flashcard
- [ ] Users can suppress a source from future influence
- [ ] Correction events are persisted with actor and timestamp
- [ ] Local refresh logic changes flashcard/source behavior based on the correction events
- [ ] Support can inspect why a flashcard or source is suppressed, hidden, or pinned

## Dependencies

- `Knowmore: Add flashcard schema, lineage, and merge support`
- `Knowmore: Build the local flashcard extraction and refresh pipeline`
- `Knowmore: Add flashcard read APIs for the online app`
- `Knowmore: Build the Knowmore page UI`

## Risks

- Without direct corrections, users will route around the system instead of improving it.
- If corrections are not durable, the same bad knowledge will reappear after reprocessing.

## Delivery Artifact

User correction events, constrained UI controls, and local-pipeline integration for flashcards and sources.

## Developer Notes

This issue should stay narrower than full manual editing. The main requirement is high-trust corrective control.
title: Knowmore: Add user correction controls for flashcards and sources

body:
## Objective

Add operator repair/reprocess controls and explicit pipeline health states for the `knowmore` and ChecklistSync maintenance system.

## Unified Context

Checklist depends on a split architecture: the online app stores user interactions and the local AI stack enriches and refreshes flashcards, checklist tasks, hashtags, and maintenance state. In that model, production support requires more than passive logging. Operators need direct recovery tools and explicit health signals.

This issue remains the operator-control umbrella, but the implementation work is now split into atomic child issues.

## Based On

Parent knowmore umbrella: #62
Related reliability roadmap: #94

## Problem

Without repair and health controls:
- stalled local processing can go unnoticed
- support teams have no bounded way to re-run company maintenance safely
- users see stale output but operators cannot act precisely

## Goal

Provide operator-visible health states plus bounded repair/reprocess actions for company knowledge and checklist maintenance pipelines.

## Scope

### In Scope
- explicit pipeline health-state model
- bounded repair and reprocess controls
- audit-safe operator actions
- cross-linking the concrete child issues that implement settings, telemetry, and watchdog behavior

### Child Execution Issues
- [ ] #95 ChecklistSync: add dedicated Checklist Settings page and cadence controls in MVP Control
- [ ] #97 ChecklistSync: expose per-lane health, lag, and backlog telemetry
- [ ] #105 MVP Control: add watchdog heartbeat and bounded restart contract for ChecklistSync

### Out of Scope
- arbitrary data editing outside defined repair actions
- broad customer-facing analytics dashboards

## Execution Prompt

Build narrow, high-value repair tools rather than vague admin power. Each operator action should have a clear purpose, idempotent behavior where possible, and audit visibility.

## Constraints

- Repair actions must preserve UUID and public-ID stability.
- Health states must reflect the split online/local architecture honestly.
- Recovery operations must not require direct Vercel-to-local connectivity if persisted polling can achieve the same result.

## Acceptance Checks

- [ ] Operators can identify whether a company pipeline is healthy, delayed, stale, or failed
- [ ] Operators can trigger bounded recovery actions safely
- [ ] Failed jobs can be retried without duplicating durable records
- [ ] Recovery actions are logged and explainable

## Dependencies

- `Knowmore: Build the local flashcard extraction and refresh pipeline`
- `Knowmore: Add flashcard read APIs for the online app`
- `Knowmore: Add backfill, observability, and failure recovery`
- Reliability roadmap #94

## Risks

- A system with no bounded recovery tools will accumulate stale knowledge silently
- Overpowered repair tools can damage lineage if they are not constrained

## Delivery Artifact

Operator repair/reprocess capability, pipeline health-state model, and audit-safe runbook integration.

## Developer Notes

This umbrella should own the operator experience, while the child issues own the implementation details.
title: Knowmore: Add operator repair/reprocess controls and pipeline health states

body:
## Objective

Add citation snapshots and conflicting-source handling to the `knowmore` knowledge layer.

## Unified Context

The `knowmore` flashcards will be built from user-provided data and agent-found online sources. Those sources are not static: URLs change, pages disappear, and different sources can disagree with each other.

If the system only stores links and current synthesized text, it will lose the evidence required to justify a flashcard later. If it merges contradictory sources without explicit handling, confidence becomes meaningless.

## Problem

Without citation snapshots and conflict handling:
- flashcards cannot reliably explain their evidence after a source changes,
- reproducibility of AI output is weak,
- contradictory evidence can be silently merged into false certainty,
- trust in confidence / impact / weight degrades quickly.

## Goal

Persist durable evidence snapshots for source-backed claims and make conflicting evidence visible in the flashcard model and processing pipeline.

## Scope

### In Scope
- citation snapshot model for source-backed evidence
- storage of normalized URL, fetched metadata, excerpt/snippet, hash, and fetch time
- linkage of flashcards to citation snapshots or equivalent durable evidence records
- conflict detection rules for contradictory or materially divergent source claims
- documented flashcard behavior when conflicts are detected, such as:
  - lower confidence
  - conflict flag / state
  - split instead of merge
  - review-required status

### Out of Scope
- browser-side citation browsing UX beyond what the initial flashcard display needs
- long-term archival infrastructure or full document warehousing
- legal/compliance policy work for internet content retention

## Execution Prompt

Treat evidence durability as part of the product contract, not a backend detail. A flashcard should still be explainable if the source URL changes next week. Likewise, disagreement between sources must affect the flashcard state explicitly instead of being hidden in the agent synthesis.

## Constraints

- The system must not rely on URL-only provenance for critical claims.
- Citation snapshots must be tied to the source record lineage.
- Conflict handling must be deterministic enough to audit.
- Conflicting evidence must not silently inflate confidence.

## Acceptance Checks

- [ ] Source-backed flashcards retain a durable evidence snapshot beyond a raw URL
- [ ] Citation snapshots capture normalized URL, snippet/excerpt, and fetch timing metadata
- [ ] Flashcards can reference the evidence records that support them
- [ ] Contradictory source inputs change flashcard state explicitly
- [ ] Merge logic documents what happens when conflict thresholds are hit

## Dependencies

- `Knowmore: Add public IDs and source provenance foundation`
- `Knowmore: Add flashcard schema, lineage, and merge support`
- `Knowmore: Build the local flashcard extraction and refresh pipeline`

## Risks

- URL-only provenance will fail as soon as external content changes.
- Undetected contradictions will produce confident-looking but weak knowledge.
- Overly aggressive conflict rules can fragment knowledge into unusable noise.

## Delivery Artifact

Citation snapshot persistence, conflict-state rules, and updated flashcard generation semantics.

## Developer Notes

This issue is intentionally upstream of trust. If it is skipped, the system may look complete but will not be auditable.
title: Knowmore: Add citation snapshots and conflicting-source handling

body:
## Objective

Generate responses to common customer objections by analyzing product and competitor data to provide effective counter-arguments.

## Problem

Sales teams face customer objections but must craft responses manually. They need AI-generated objection responses that are tailored to their specific product and competitive advantages.

## Goal

Build AI objection handling that:
- Identifies common objections in the industry
- Generates tailored responses for each
- Highlights product strengths vs competitors
- Provides reframing techniques
- Creates follow-up suggestions

## Scope

### In
- Common objection library by industry
- Product vs competitor analysis
- Response generation (5-10 common objections)
- Reframing techniques
- Follow-up suggestions

### Out
- Automated objection detection
- Real-time call assistance
- CRM integration

## Constraints
- Use existing local AI models
- Requires product and competitor data
- Responses stored for review

## Acceptance Checks
- Objections page shows common responses
- Each response has rationale
- Product differentiators highlighted
- Works in light and dark mode

## Dependencies
- Product data (existing)
- Competitor data (existing)
- Existing AI pipeline

## Risks
- Generic responses without enough context
- May not cover all industry-specific objections

## Delivery Artifact
- New: src/app/[companyId]/objections/page.tsx
- Update: brain.js for objection handling
- API: /api/objections

## Developer Notes
- Group by objection category
- Show confidence level
- Allow editing and saving
title: AI: Objection Handling

body:
## Objective

Recommend best marketing channels based on customer data and industry analysis.

## Problem

Users need to know which marketing channels will be most effective for their target audience but have no data-driven guidance. They guess at channel selection.

## Goal

Build AI channel recommendation that:
- Analyzes customer demographics
- Reviews industry benchmarks
- Scores channels by expected ROI
- Provides channel-specific tactics
- Suggests budget allocation

## Scope

### In
- Customer data analysis
- Industry classification
- Channel scoring (email, social, content, paid, etc)
- Budget recommendations
- Tactics per channel

## Objective

Allow users to export their task list (NBA items) as a CSV file for external reporting, spreadsheet analysis, and data backup purposes.

## Problem

Users need to share their task data with stakeholders who may not have access to the application, or want to perform their own analysis in Excel/Google Sheets. Currently there is no way to export data from the application.

## Goal

Add CSV export functionality that allows users to download their task list as a properly formatted CSV file with all relevant fields.

## Scope

### In
- Export button on NBA page
- CSV generation with headers
- Download trigger in browser
- Include: task name, description, ICE score, status, created date, acceptance date

### Out
- Scheduled exports
- Email delivery
- Bulk export of all data types

## Constraints
- Must work with existing NBAItem model
- Must handle special characters in CSV (quotes, commas)
- File must be properly encoded (UTF-8)

## Acceptance Checks
- Export button visible on NBA page
- Clicking exports CSV file
- CSV opens correctly in Excel/Google Sheets
- All relevant fields included
- Proper escaping of special characters

## Dependencies
- NBAItem API (GET /api/nba)
- Existing NBA page structure
- Browser download API

## Risks
- Large datasets may timeout or create large files
- Need to handle empty data gracefully

## Delivery Artifact
- Update: src/app/[companyId]/nba/page.tsx
- New: src/lib/export-csv.ts utility
- API: Existing /api/nba endpoint (no changes needed)

## Developer Notes
- Use existing page patterns from products/customers
- Use native Blob API for file generation
- Test with various data lengths and special characters

## Objective

Provide users with comprehensive visibility into their task management performance through an analytics dashboard that displays completion stats, acceptance rates, and ICE score trends over time.

## Problem

Users currently have no way to measure their productivity or understand how their acceptance rates evolve. They cannot track ICE score trends or identify patterns in their task completion behavior.

## Goal

Create an Analytics page accessible from the dashboard that displays:
- Task completion statistics (total, completed, pending)
- Acceptance rate over time (% of NBA items accepted)
- ICE score trends (visual chart showing score distribution)
- Time-based filtering (weekly, monthly, quarterly views)

## Scope

### In
- Analytics dashboard page at /analytics
- Completion stats widget
- Acceptance rate chart
- ICE score trend visualization
- Time period filters

### Out
- Predictive analytics
- AI-powered insights
- Export functionality (covered in #37)

## Constraints
- Must work with existing data models (NBAItem, Product, Customer, Competitor)
- Must respect existing authentication/authorization
- Must be responsive for mobile viewing

## Acceptance Checks
- Analytics page accessible from dashboard navigation
- Shows total task count, completed count, pending count
- Acceptance rate displayed as percentage
- ICE score chart renders correctly
- Time filter changes displayed data
- Works in both light and dark mode

## Dependencies
- NBAItem model with status and ICE score fields
- Company data already loaded
- Existing dashboard layout
